summary: The mechanism rests on a misreading of issue_tile: each warp-wide cp.async already touches all four 32-byte sectors of every 128-byte K/V line (chunks 0,2,4,6 at offsets 0/32/64/96 on j=0, then 1,3,5,7 on j=1), so DRAM already fetches each row once and an L2::128B hint cannot remove a transaction; the predicted 0-5% is also below the 6% run-to-run drift on full decode_32, so one run cannot be interpreted.
justification: A. In master's issue_tile, thread tid handles token tt = tid>>2 and 16-byte chunks c = 2*(tid&3)+j. For j=0 one warp instruction covers 8 tokens x chunks {0,2,4,6}, which are byte offsets 0,32,64,96: one 16-byte piece in each of the line's four 32-byte sectors. Every sector of every row is therefore requested from L2 by the first instruction, and the j=1 instruction (chunks 1,3,5,7) hits the same sectors, which are already in flight or resident. DRAM traffic is already one 128-byte line per K or V row. ROW = 128 and rows sit at kc + row*128, so a line is exactly one row: a 128-byte prefetch brings in nothing new, and because page_size=1 gathers scattered rows, neighbouring rows cannot benefit either. The hypothesis says the two instructions are '64 bytes apart' (each a contiguous half-row), but that is not the code's mapping. The sibling splitkv-full-line-gather-mapping makes the same mistake ('two sectors of each line'). Profile context: kernel A takes 111.8 us at decode_16 (SoL 63.2 us for the whole shape) and 245.9 us at decode_32 (SoL 126.4 us), so it is roughly 1.8-1.9x off the floor and a real target, but this change cannot account for any of that gap. The expected directions are consistent with TASK.md, since only full decode_16/32 run kernel A, and those flat elsewhere. Weakest link: the premise that each row costs two DRAM transactions today. It is false on this code, so the expected effect is about 0 and sits inside the documented 6% median drift on full decode_32. A gain would be noise and a loss would be noise.
confounders: full-decode-cuda-gather-splitkv (landed): introduces the exact issue_tile mapping and 16-byte cp.async.cg loads the hypothesis modifies; its interleaved chunk mapping is what already makes every instruction touch all four sectors, so the hint is redundant specifically because of how that patch laid out the copies.

sliding-deep-splits-on-cuda-splitkv (landed, current best): touches only sliding shapes, but it moved full decode_32 within the run, and the noted ~6% drift on full decode_32 between identical runs swamps a 0-5% prediction.
interference: No companion makes a single run readable here, because the problem is the premise and not interference. An ab-revert of full-decode-cuda-gather-splitkv would remove the kernel entirely. A control that changes only the module name would just measure noise. If the author still wants to test L2 promotion, the useful experiment is a non-scored ncu comparison of kernel A's dram__sectors_read and lts__t_sectors_srcunit_tex_op_read, with and without the qualifier. That should show identical DRAM sector counts. A scored check is not the way to test it.
open_questions: Hold the sibling splitkv-full-line-gather-mapping on the same grounds? Its stated reason ('two sectors of each line' per instruction) is also wrong. Its remap could still help L2 request coalescing a little (one instruction covering full lines for 4 tokens instead of half of each sector for 8), but it should be re-justified on request count, not DRAM transactions.
If full-cuda-onelaunch-warpspec-bulk-gather (running) lands and self-checks, kernel A is replaced for these shapes and both splitkv-gather micro-tunings become moot.

Kernel A's remaining ~1.9x gap to SoL is more likely latency or occupancy bound: 4-stage ring x 16 KB at 2 CTAs/SM gives about 128 KB in flight per SM, plus per-tile __syncthreads and mma.sync compute. A deeper ring or more bytes in flight per SM is a better-founded lever than cache hints.
